strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution: the paper identifies a genuine misalignment in typographic-attack research, where robustness has been pursued via text-ignoring defenses that sacrifice text-reading ability, and formalizes 'selective text use' as a unified task (RIO-VQA).

Benchmark construction is carefully controlled: same-scene counterfactuals (Object/Text x Clean/Attack) isolate selective text use from confounders, with hierarchical negative sampling for MC questions, three semantic difficulty levels for object attacks, and distance-controlled text attacks that avoid ill-posed (near-occluding) cases.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: six LVLMs across scales, both inference-time (CoT) and training-based (IT-RT) defense baselines, ablations on LoRA placement (interesting finding that selective text use is primarily learned in the language model), attack-level analysis, attention visualization, cross-domain generalization to Typo-D and document/chart VQA, and a data-size ablation.

The proposed RIO-RT defense demonstrates a meaningful result: robustness gains comparable to ignore-text training while preserving and even improving text-VQA accuracy, directly validating the paper's central claim about the robustness/reading trade-off.

Good reproducibility posture: full data-generation code promised for release, detailed pipeline description (prompts, rendering configs, metrics), and cheap construction cost (~3 hours). Limitations section acknowledges the VQA-only scope.
weaknesses: The benchmark inherits limitations of its single base dataset: it is built entirely on TextVQA/Open Images, with template-generated object questions (one fixed OE prompt, fixed MC templates). Object-centric QA is thus fairly artificial, and noisy/inherited TextVQA pairs are visible in the appendix (e.g., 'what kind of beer is this?' with answer '22' on a baseball image), raising data-quality concerns that are not quantified.

The R-CLIP-M metric is somewhat ad hoc (difference of top-5 CLIP text-similarity matches) and can conflate label selection with evaluation; ground-truth labels are themselves chosen by CLIP similarity, potentially injecting CLIP bias into both training and evaluation.

The technical novelty of the defense is modest: RIO-RT is essentially balanced SFT over Obj-Attack and Text-Attack data, and its advantage over IT-RT on the object branch is marginal (e.g., 98.1 vs 97.9 MC accuracy on LLaVA-1.5-7B). The main gain (preserving text reading) is arguably an expected consequence of including text-attack data rather than a new mechanism; the paper's framing somewhat overstates this as acquiring a 'genuinely new capability'.

There is a risk of circularity between the training and evaluation distributions: RIO-RT is trained on RIO-Bench splits and evaluated on RIO-Bench, so its headline within-domain gains do not by themselves demonstrate generalizable selective text use; the strongest evidence (Typo-D, document VQA) is relegated to the appendix.

Attack realism is limited: single font (DejaVuSans), flat text overlays without perspective/lighting/occlusion modeling, which is well behind the state of the art in typographic attack synthesis (e.g., SceneTAP) the paper itself cites; robustness conclusions may not transfer to physical or photorealistic attacks.

Several details are deferred to the appendix (metric definitions, CoT reproduction, key-text matching), and the main-paper text is at times promotional in tone ('fundamental misalignment', 'first structural foundation'), which should be tempered given that related concurrent datasets (e.g., SCAM) exist.

strengths: The task formulation (RIO-VQA) is well-motivated: the observation that prior typographic-attack evaluations implicitly reward text-ignoring behavior, creating a misalignment with real-world LVLM deployments that require joint object/text reasoning, is a genuine and clearly articulated gap.

The same-scene counterfactual design (Object/Text × Clean/Attack on identical images from TextVQA/Open Images dual annotations) is a sound methodological choice that isolates selective text use from confounding factors better than combining unrelated datasets.

The empirical study is broad: six LVLMs across scales and architectures, inference-time (CoT) and training-based defenses, attack-difficulty ablations, LoRA-placement ablations, attention visualizations, and cross-domain generalization to Typo-D and text-centric VQA benchmarks (AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA).

The appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail: dataset statistics, exact prompts, attack rendering configuration, metric definitions (R-CLIP-M), computational costs, and a stated commitment to release the data-generation code.

The finding that language-model tuning (not vision-encoder modification) drives selective text use, supported by the LoRA ablation, is an interesting and potentially useful insight that contrasts with prior vision-centric defenses.
weaknesses: The core defense (RIO-RT) is methodologically thin: it is standard SFT on a balanced mixture of the benchmark's own training split. The claimed 'novel, adaptive, context-aware capability' largely amounts to fine-tuning on in-distribution data whose question phrasing (object-centric vs. text-centric) directly signals whether text should be read or ignored. The model may be learning a simple question-type-to-behavior mapping rather than deep contextual reasoning; the paper does not test this with held-out question types, paraphrases, or adversarially reworded prompts.

There is a train/test circularity concern: RIO-Bench's validation split is constructed with the identical pipeline (same templates, same rendering policy, same Llama-3 distractor generator) as the training split, and RIO-RT is evaluated on it. Generalization is shown only on external benchmarks, where the object-side gains are inconsistent (e.g., LLaVA-1.5-13B shows no clear Typo-D improvement and text-centric VQA results are mixed).

Benchmark quality issues are visible in the released examples: the rendered attack text is often tiny, low-contrast, and barely legible even to humans (e.g., 'Cowboy hat', 'Traffic sign' overlays in Figs. 6–11), raising doubts about whether Text-Attack 'hard' cases measure selective text use or just OCR sensitivity. Also, object ground truth is selected via CLIP similarity over Open Images labels, which can inject annotation noise (e.g., 'Billboard' vs. 'Traffic sign' confusions).

The R-CLIP-M metric is ad hoc: a difference of top-5 CLIP text-similarities conflates correctness and attack resistance in a single scalar whose scale and interpretability are not validated; no human study or correlation analysis with human judgments is provided.

Novelty relative to prior work is moderate: Cheng et al. [8] already proposed CoT defenses against typographic attacks on LVLMs, and the conceptual point that robustness vs. text-reading involves a trade-off is fairly intuitive; the main technical novelty is the benchmark construction, and the 'first attempt' claims for text-centric attacks are difficult to verify. The headline result (ignore-text training degrades reading) is somewhat predictable and the RIO-RT improvement over IT-RT on Text-VQA is the expected outcome of including Text-Attack data in training.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported from single runs (no seeds, no variance), the metrics on open-ended Text-VQA with 10 fixed TextVQA answers are noisy, and several relative-gain claims (e.g., '+570%') are driven by near-zero pretrained baselines, which inflates the apparent benefit.

Some baselines are missing or weak: no comparison with simpler prompting alternatives (e.g., a neutral instruction to answer 'based on the image content, reading text only when the question requires it'), no closed-source/frontier models that are most relevant to deployment, and no adaptive-attack evaluation (an attacker who knows the defense).

Writing is generally clear but repetitive: the 'text-agnostic vs. selective' framing and the misalignment claim are restated many times, and the abstract's project-page URL is missing, suggesting incomplete polish.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and clearly articulated gap: typographic-attack research has focused on object recognition, implicitly pushing defenses toward text-ignoring behavior, while real deployments require joint object/text reasoning. The 'selective text use' framing is a novel and useful concept for the field.

RIO-Bench is well designed. The same-scene counterfactual construction (crossing question type and attack condition over identical images) is a methodologically sound way to isolate selective text use from confounds, and the choice of TextVQA+Open Images dual annotations is a clever, defensible instantiation. The pipeline is also cheap (~3 hours) and reusable on other dual-annotation datasets.

The experimental evidence is broad and convincing: six LVLMs across architectures and scales, multiple attack difficulty levels, both MC and open-ended formats, inference-time (CoT) and training-based (IT-RT) baselines, LoRA placement ablations, attention visualizations, data-size ablations, and—importantly—generalization experiments on external benchmarks (Typo-D, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA). The cross-domain results meaningfully strengthen the claim that RIO-RT teaches a transferable capability rather than benchmark-specific memorization.

RIO-RT is a simple but well-motivated contribution: balanced exposure to Obj-Attack and Text-Attack data yields robustness without sacrificing (and often improving) text reading, directly demonstrating the paper's core thesis about the trade-off in existing defenses.

The supplementary material is thorough and reproducible: explicit prompts, key-text localization heuristics, distance-controlled attack placement, exact metric definitions (R-CLIP-M, VQA accuracy), and a stated commitment to releasing data-generation code.
The paper is clearly written, with good figures (taxonomy, pipeline, attention maps) that support the argument, and it includes an honest limitations discussion.

The contribution type is appropriately Datasets/Benchmarks with an associated method; the assessment here does not demand state-of-the-art on external leaderboards, and the evidence matches the claims.
weaknesses: Attack realism: the typographic attacks are digital overlays rendered in a single font (DejaVuSans) with uniformly sampled color and placement. This is far simpler than physical or scene-coherent attacks (e.g., SceneTAP), so conclusions about 'robustness' may overstate security relevance. The paper acknowledges some prior work in this space but does not test its conclusions against more realistic attack generators.

The benchmark is instantiated from a single source (TextVQA/Open Images). The generalization experiments evaluate models trained on RIO-Bench, but the benchmark's own diversity (scene types, question styles, attack distribution) is limited; claims about 'selective text use' as a general capability would be stronger with a second instantiation of the pipeline.

The proposed R-CLIP-M metric is somewhat ad hoc: subtracting CLIP-M@5 similarity to the attack word from correctness can conflate semantically near-synonymous answers with attack success, and CLIP text similarity itself is a noisy proxy. A human-study validation of the metric (or at least its correlation with human judgments) is missing.

Baseline coverage is thin on the defense side: essentially one inference-time method (CoT) and one adapted training baseline (IT-RT). Given the claim that 'existing defenses fail to balance robustness and reading,' stronger comparisons to other LVLM-applicable mitigations (e.g., prompt ensembles, system-prompt variants, or other reasoning-based defenses) would be needed for the strongest version of this claim.

The training/evaluation design leaves open a shortcut concern: RIO-RT is trained on the same distribution (and difficulty structure, Hard attacks) as the test split, so some of the robustness gains may reflect distribution-specific fitting rather than learned selective text use; the Typo-D transfer result mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

Minor: several typos/presentation issues ('providessame-scene', figure quality, some garbled text in examples where the question does not match the image, e.g., 'what kind of beer is this?' on a whiteboard image in Figs. 9–11) suggest some construction noise that should be audited; example-level annotation errors could affect VQA accuracy measurements.

strengths: Contribution type: although not explicitly declared, this is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper (with a modest baseline defense), not a new-algorithm paper; judged on that basis, the contribution is substantial.

Clear, well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap—typographic-attack robustness has been evaluated object-centrically, making it impossible to tell whether defenses preserve text reading. The read-or-ignore framing is intuitive and practically relevant (autonomous driving, embodied AI).

Strong benchmark design: the same-scene counterfactual structure (scene fixed, varying question intent and text condition) is a thoughtful way to reduce confounds, and the dual-annotation insight (TextVQA QA + Open Images labels) is an elegant construction mechanism.
Benchmark quality is validated with a human audit (400 samples, 3 annotators, high inter-annotator agreement: Gwet's AC1 0.89–0.94), which is more than most automated VQA benchmarks provide.

Evidence is comprehensive for a benchmark paper: 6 older LVLMs plus modern families (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5 at multiple scales) and closed-source frontier models (GPT-5.4, Gemini-2.5-Pro); two attack types (controlled overlays and SceneTAP generative insertions); ablations on attack difficulty, LoRA placement, and training data size; generalization to Typo-D and external text-VQA datasets.
The R-CLIP-M metric is a sensible, well-justified fix to CLIP-M's blindness to attack-word-induced bias.

The central empirical finding—that object-centric defenses gain robustness by suppressing text sensitivity, and that this failure mode is invisible under object-centric evaluation alone—is a substantive, actionable insight for the robustness community, and the attention analysis gives mechanistic support.
RIO-RT is honestly positioned as a minimal reference baseline, and limitations are meaningfully discussed (scope to LVLM×VQA, fixed training recipe, restricted threat models).
weaknesses: Label-noise risk in automated construction: ground-truth object labels are selected via CLIP similarity ranking over Open Images annotations, which introduces a potential circularity (CLIP-scored GT may favor what CLIP-like models perceive), and MC negatives are hierarchy-derived templates. The human audit partially mitigates this, but it is a 400-sample audit of a 34,826-sample evaluation set.

Object-centric questions are template-generated rather than naturally authored, so the object branch is less linguistically diverse than the text branch (which reuses TextVQA questions); this asymmetry could subtly affect cross-setting comparisons.

The headline defense comparison (RIO-RT vs. IT-RT) varies only the data mixture under an identical SFT recipe, so the finding that balanced training preserves text reading is partly predictable—models trained on Text-Attack instances retain text-reading by construction. The more informative claim (selective read-or-ignore, rather than label memorization) is supported by SceneTAP and Typo-D transfer but could be probed harder, e.g., with held-out attack word distributions.

Several evaluation columns involve attack types seen during training (marked * in Tab. 3), inflating the trained models' reported averages relative to original/CoT baselines; the unseen-condition (SceneTAP, out-of-benchmark) results are the fairest comparison and should be foregrounded more.

Only one inference-time defense (CoT) exists for LVLMs, so the claim about a general 'trade-off' in existing defenses rests largely on the authors' own IT-RT adaptation of a CLIP defense; the external-validity of the trade-off for third-party defenses is limited.

The 'fundamental misalignment' framing is somewhat strong: the observation that text-suppressing defenses degrade text reading was already visible in prior object-centric work; the benchmark makes the trade-off measurable rather than discovering an entirely new phenomenon.

Scope is confined to TextVQA/Open Images scenes; all results derive from one image domain (natural scenes with incidental text), so claims about real-world deployment (e.g., driving) are extrapolations beyond what is measured.

strengths: The core motivation is genuine and well-articulated: prior typographic-attack defenses are evaluated only on object-centric tasks, so it is impossible to tell whether robustness is achieved by selective distractor filtering or by wholesale suppression of text sensitivity. Framing 'read-or-ignore' behavior as a joint evaluation requirement is a useful reframing of the problem.

The same-scene counterfactual design (holding the image fixed while varying question intent and text condition) is a sound methodological choice that reduces dataset/scene confounds, and the paper is careful to explain why naively combining object-VQA and text-VQA datasets would obscure the phenomenon being studied.

Evidence appropriate to a benchmark contribution: a large training and evaluation split (241K/35K), two attack regimes (controlled overlays plus scene-coherent SceneTAP insertions with OCR-preservation safeguards), difficulty levels grounded in the Open Images class hierarchy, a human audit with three annotators, 400 samples, and reported inter-annotator agreement (Gwet's AC1 0.89–0.94), plus attention-map analysis offering a mechanistic interpretation of the trade-off.

Evaluation coverage is broad and current: six open-source LVLMs of varied architectures/scales, scaling analysis for Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 families, two frontier closed-source models, and out-of-benchmark generalization to Typo-D and text-centric VQA datasets (AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA), which partially mitigates the concern that the defense learns benchmark-specific artifacts.

Honest scoping: RIO-RT is presented as a minimal reference baseline rather than a novel method, SceneTAP-based subsets are evaluation-only, and the limitations section is candid about scope (LVLM×VQA only, single training recipe, fixed threat models).

The paper is effectively a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution even though no type is declared; judged under that lens, the construction pipeline, quality validation, and release plan (training split included) are consistent with community norms.
weaknesses: The object-centric ground-truth pipeline is noisy by construction: a single GT class is chosen from multi-label Open Images annotations via CLIP image-text similarity, and MC distractors are sampled from a hierarchy. While the human audit (96–98% 'desirable' judgments) partially validates this, 400 samples out of ~34K evaluation instances is a thin audit, and CLIP-based GT selection may systematically bias question difficulty; per-question error analysis on the audit failures is not provided.

The headline defense result (Obj-Attack accuracy jumping to ~98% across all models after fine-tuning) raises a shortcut-learning concern: the Overlay-Attack uses a single fixed font (DejaVuSans), a fixed size range (24–32 px), and eight colors, so models may simply learn to discount the distinctive rendered-overlay artifact rather than acquire genuine read-or-ignore behavior. The SceneTAP transfer is encouraging, but the paper does not test held-out rendering styles (fonts, colors, physical photographs) to rule out artifact detection.

R-CLIP-M is an ad hoc metric: subtracting attack-word retrieval from GT-label retrieval can produce negative or uninterpretable values, and there is no sensitivity analysis over K, the CLIP model choice, or how the metric correlates with human judgments of open-ended answers.

The central empirical claim (object-centric defenses trade robustness for text reading) rests largely on the authors' own constructed IT-RT baseline, since only one prior LVLM defense (CoT prompting of Cheng et al.) exists and could be evaluated. The 'fundamental misalignment' framing is therefore supported more by the paper's own training experiment than by an independent survey of existing defenses, which weakens the claim's generality.

Benchmark domain coverage is narrow: everything derives from TextVQA/Open Images natural scene images. Extensibility to other dual-annotation datasets is claimed but not demonstrated, and the text-attack generation relies on a single LLM (Llama-3) for distractor phrases, whose diversity and difficulty calibration are not validated beyond a two-level spatial-distance heuristic.

Presentation issues: Table 3 is extremely dense with overlapping annotations (arrows, asterisks, difficulty levels) and hard to parse; Fig. 3 compresses six models into small subplots with cramped axes. The closed-source evaluation covers only two models, and an apparent typo ('GPT-5.4') undermines confidence in that section.

Missing ablations on benchmark validity: no analysis of how MC question quality degrades when CLIP GT selection is uncertain (e.g., low-margin cases), and no comparison of Overlay-Attack results against a trivial baseline that ignores all inserted text everywhere, which would contextualize the absolute robustness numbers.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine blind spot in typographic-attack evaluation - object-centric protocols cannot distinguish between robustness achieved by selectively filtering distractors versus globally suppressing text sensitivity - and formalizes the read-or-ignore task to expose this.

The same-scene counterfactual benchmark design is a solid methodological contribution: by holding the scene fixed and varying only question intent and text condition across four matched subsets, confounds are substantially reduced relative to naively combining object-VQA and text-VQA datasets.

Comprehensive and careful benchmark construction: dual annotations from TextVQA/Open Images, hierarchy-based negative sampling with difficulty levels, both controlled overlays and scene-coherent generative insertions (SceneTAP), explicit safeguards to avoid occluding answer-bearing text, and a large train/val split (241K/34K).

Evidence quality is above average for a benchmark paper: a 400-sample human audit with three annotators and high inter-annotator agreement (Gwet's AC1 0.89-0.94), evaluation across six open-source LVLMs plus modern scaling families and closed-source frontier models, out-of-benchmark transfer to TypoD and four text-centric VQA datasets, ablations on LoRA placement and training-data size, and attention-map analysis that supports the 'selective disregard' interpretation.
The proposed R-CLIP-M metric is a thoughtful adaptation that penalizes attack-word-induced bias in open-ended answers, addressing a real weakness of naive CLIP-M under typographic attacks.

The IT-RT vs. RIO-RT comparison directly operationalizes the paper's central claim: object-only robust training degrades text reading (dramatically in some cases, e.g., -48% to -75% Text-VQA), while balanced training preserves it, making the trade-off concrete rather than anecdotal.

Appropriate for a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution type: the benchmark itself, not a new algorithm, is the primary contribution, and the defense baseline (RIO-RT) is presented honestly as a minimal reference rather than oversold; limitations are discussed candidly.
weaknesses: Benchmark scope is narrow: everything derives from TextVQA scenes with one QA per image and Open Images class labels. Object-centric questions are template-generated from a restricted class vocabulary, which may not represent the diversity of real object-VQA; the paper acknowledges extensibility but provides no evidence of generalization to other source datasets.

Attack realism is only partially addressed: Overlay-Attacks are synthetic digital overlays, and although SceneTAP insertions are included as evaluation-only, the base images remain static TextVQA photos - no physical-world validation, no multi-text or adversarially optimized distractors.

Potential train/val contamination concern: training and validation splits come from the same 21,953/3,166 image scenes constructed with the same automated pipeline (CLIP-scored GT labels, LLM-generated distractors, template questions). Fine-tuning on pipeline artifacts could teach dataset-specific regularities rather than read-or-ignore behavior; out-of-distribution transfer is shown only at the coarse TypoD level.

The R-CLIP-M metric introduces its own confounds: it depends on the choice of CLIP model and K, and subtracting attack-word retrieval scores may mispenalize answers that legitimately mention multiple objects; sensitivity to these hyperparameters is not analyzed.

The defense comparison is somewhat asymmetric: CoT [7] is the only prior LVLM defense and is inference-time only, while IT-RT is the authors' own construction (an adaptation of a CLIP-era method) rather than a strong established baseline; conclusions about 'prior text-ignoring baselines' rest partly on a baseline the authors built.

RIO-RT results show nontrivial variance across models (e.g., SmolVLM-2B Text-Attack stays roughly flat, LLaVA-1.5-13B Text-Clean drops 2%), and the paper does not characterize when balanced training fails; a finer-grained discussion of failure cases would strengthen the claims.

Some clarity issues: Fig. 3 and Tab. 3 are dense and hard to parse; the contribution of the 'Findings' bullets would benefit from statistical significance or variance estimates given only single-run training.

Reproducibility is not explicitly addressed in the manuscript: there is no stated commitment to releasing the benchmark, code, and trained checkpoints, which is essential for a paper whose primary contribution is a community benchmark.
